questions.question: What spatial design was used to census Q. costaricensis seedlings, and what was the observed bamboo-stem density range?

options.A: Four 400-m² plots subdivided into 64 quadrats each; bamboo ranged from 0 to 14 stems/m²
options.B: Four 64-m² plots subdivided into 400 quadrats each; bamboo ranged from 0 to 14 stems/plot
options.C: Ten 400-m² plots subdivided into 20 quadrats each; bamboo ranged from 2 to 14 stems/m²
options.D: Four 20-m² plots subdivided into 64 quadrats; bamboo ranged from 0 to 20 stems/m²

questions.rationale: The study used four 20×20 m plots, each split into 64 2.5×2.5 m quadrats, where bamboo density naturally varied from zero to 14 stems per square meter.
questions.evidence_quote: We set four 400-m 2 plots (20 x 20 m) within CMBS.

questions.question: How did the investigators define the only masting recruitment event analyzed?

options.A: The 2014 fruiting year; new seedlings recorded in 2015 were treated as its cohort
options.B: The 2016 fruiting year; only seedlings first seen in 2017 were analyzed
options.C: Both 2014 and 2016 were treated as masting years with equal recruitment
options.D: The 2015 census was treated as a masting event because all adults fruited then

questions.rationale: Although the oak fruited in 2014 and 2016, fewer than 15% of adults reproduced in 2016; 2014 was therefore the only masting event, with new 2015 recruits assigned to it.
questions.evidence_quote: therefore we considered the 2014 fruiting year as the only masting event during the study period.

questions.question: Which spatial-statistical transformation was used to examine seedling aggregation in the 2014 cohort?

options.A: The univariate Ripley L(t) transform, L(t)=(K(t)/π)^{0.5}
options.B: A bivariate Moran's I transform of the 2015 recruitment counts
options.C: A nearest-neighbor G-function with a Poisson distribution
options.D: A semivariogram of seedling height within each quadrat

questions.rationale: The methods specify the transformed univariate Ripley K function for spatial distribution of the 2014 seedlings.
questions.evidence_quote: We analyzed the spatial distribution of seedlings in our plots using the L(t)=(K(t)/π) 0.5 transformation of the univariate Ripley's

questions.question: What model structure was used for annual seedling survival, and which grouping factors were random effects?

options.A: A binomial GLMM with quadrat and census year as random effects
options.B: A quasi-Poisson GLMM with plot and adult tree as random effects
options.C: A linear mixed model with seedling and species as random effects
options.D: A logistic regression with no random effects and unstandardized predictors

questions.rationale: The three-year annual survival probability was modeled with a binomial GLMM, including quadrat and census year as random effects.
questions.evidence_quote: We modeled the annual probability of seedling survival for three years between 2014 and 2017

questions.question: What survival pattern was observed across years, and which two measured factors reduced survival?

options.A: Survival declined from 73.2% to 64.38% to 63.8%; bamboo density and herbivory reduced it
options.B: Survival rose from 63.8% to 64.38% to 73.2%; height and density reduced it
options.C: Survival stayed near 73%; adult proximity and seedling density reduced it
options.D: Survival declined from 73.2% to 63.8% to 64.38%; herbivory alone reduced it

questions.rationale: Annual survival decreased from 2015 through 2017, with bamboo density and herbivory both negatively affecting survival.
questions.evidence_quote: Annual seedling survival decreased slightly over the study period, from 73.2% in 2015 to 64.38% (2016) and 63.8% (2017).

questions.question: How did the effect of conspecific seedling density on survival depend on bamboo density?

options.A: High seedling density increased survival below 2.4 bamboo stems/m² but decreased it at higher bamboo density
options.B: High seedling density decreased survival below 2.4 stems/m² but increased it above that threshold
options.C: Seedling density had no effect at any bamboo density
options.D: The positive density effect occurred only when bamboo exceeded 14 stems/m²

questions.rationale: A significant density interaction reversed the direction of the seedling-density effect across the stated bamboo threshold.
questions.evidence_quote: high seedling density significantly increased seedling survival at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems per m 2 ), and decreased survival at higher bamboo densities

questions.question: What relationship between distance to the nearest adult and seedling survival best fit the data?

options.A: A negative quadratic relationship, with survival highest at intermediate distances
options.B: A linear decline, with survival highest directly beneath adults
options.C: A positive linear relationship, with survival highest farthest from adults
options.D: No relationship, because conspecific distance was excluded from the model

questions.rationale: The fitted polynomial indicated lower survival at the extremes and a peak at intermediate distance from adult trees.
questions.evidence_quote: The effect of near adults on seedling survival was best described by a negative polynomial function; seedling survival was highest at intermediate distances from adults

questions.question: What was the result for recruitment in 2015 after the 2014 masting event?

options.A: There were 1,578 recruits; recruitment increased with seedling density but not adult or bamboo density
options.B: There were 2,031 recruits; recruitment increased with adult density but not seedling density
options.C: There were 55 recruits; recruitment was negatively related to bamboo only
options.D: There were 1,578 recruits; recruitment decreased with seedling density and increased with bamboo

questions.rationale: The 2015 census recorded 1,578 new recruits, with recruitment associated positively with conspecific seedling density but not adult-tree or Chusquea density.

questions.question: What explanation did the authors propose for the apparent lack of CNDD despite ubiquitous herbivory?

options.A: Predator satiation after masting may weaken negative density effects, and adult ectomycorrhizal transfer may facilitate nearby seedlings
options.B: Herbivores were absent from the plots, and oak seeds were wind dispersed
options.C: Seedling aggregation was an artifact of the 2015 recruitment census
options.D: CNDD was masked by complete resistance to leaf damage in all seedlings

questions.rationale: The discussion invokes predator satiation and possible ectomycorrhizal facilitation from nearby adults as explanations for weak or absent CNDD.
questions.evidence_quote: the high density of this endemic oak tree in the Costa Rican montane forests is likely the result of predator satiation and adult facilitation through ectomycorrhyzal transference from nearby conspecifics

questions.question: Which factors did the authors identify as important local regulators despite the absence of CNDD?

options.A: Herbivory and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo
options.B: Distance to adults and conspecific seedling density
options.C: Soil nutrients and annual rainfall only
options.D: Adult basal area and pathogen infection only

questions.rationale: The conclusion attributes local density regulation to herbivory and bamboo density rather than conspecific negative density dependence.
questions.evidence_quote: Herbivory and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo appear to be important factors controlling seedling density of this species
